references.text: The psalmist asks who is like the Lord, who rules over the raging sea and stills its waves – this points to Jesus' authority over wind and water.
God commands the storm and calms it, so that the waves settle and the people rejoice. Jesus does what Yahweh does in this psalm, underscoring his divine identity.
God quiets the roaring of the seas and the clamor of the nations. Jesus' power over natural forces reflects God's sovereign rule over creation.
God speaks of setting boundaries for the sea and stilling its proud waves. Jesus displays the same divine authority over natural forces.
Matthew's parallel account of the calming of the storm, where the disciples marvel and ask: "What kind of man is this, that even wind and sea obey him?"
Mark's parallel account where Jesus rebukes the wind and says to the sea "Be still!", and the disciples are filled with great fear and ask who he is.
The preceding verse tells how Jesus rebuked the wind and waves, and they ceased – the context for the disciples' wonder and question about his identity.
Even though the earth shakes and mountains tremble, the believer need not fear, for God is our refuge. Jesus' question "Where is your faith?" reflects this trust in God's power amid the storm.
Jesus says to Peter "You of little faith, why did you doubt?" – the same theme of lacking faith in dangerous situations on the water.
In Mark's parallel, Jesus asks the disciples: "Why are you so afraid? Do you still have no faith?" – a direct parallel to Jesus' question about their faith.
All the earth shall fear the Lord, for he spoke and it came to be, he commanded and it stood firm. Jesus' words commanding natural forces reveal his divine creative power.
The Lord rebukes the sea and dries it up; he rules over all the waters. Jesus' dominion over wind and water shows that he acts with God's own authority over creation.
